title: Tisha B'Av
hookLine: a fast of mourning for both Temples and later sorrows, with Lamentations read sitting on the floor

cards: One word, chanted slowly in a dim room: eichah. How. It's the first word of the book of Lamentations, and in Hebrew it's also the book's name.
On this summer night the curtain has been taken off the ark. People sit on the floor, or on low stools, some in socks or canvas sneakers. No one greets anyone with a hello.
The reader goes on by a small light, verse after verse. The whole room sits low, as if someone has died. In a way, someone has.

teach.h: TISHA B'AV: THE NINTH OF AV.
teach.b: Tisha B'Av means the ninth of Av, a day of mourning.
On this date, the Mishnah says, both Temples in Jerusalem were destroyed: the first by Babylon, the second by Rome.
The Mishnah adds other sorrows to the date, and later tradition remembered more on it, among them the expulsion of the Jews from Spain. So it became the day to mourn many losses at once.

It's kept like mourning for a close relative. A fast, from sunset to nightfall, like Yom Kippur, but it gives way to health: anyone ill, pregnant, nursing or at risk asks a doctor and a rabbi. No leather shoes.
No washing for pleasure. People sit on the floor or low stools, as mourners do in the week after a funeral. Then comes Lamentations, five short poems of grief over Jerusalem.
It opens: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!" Even Torah study, usually a joy, is limited to sad texts. Still, the day isn't only despair.
The rabbis asked why the Second Temple fell, and answered: baseless hatred, people hating each other for nothing. So the day becomes a call to repair. At midday, mourners may rise from the floor.
An old tradition says that on Tisha B'Av, of all days, the redeemer is born.

teach.h: RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.
teach.b: And near its end, Lamentations pleads to begin again: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." In the reading, that verse is said again after the last one, so it ends there.
That closes the walk through the year, from the calendar and the moon to, today, the floor.

how: On Tisha B'Av, many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations and mournful poems (kinot) chanted in dim light.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis after the Second Temple fell. people ask you why it happened. what reason does the Talmud give?
o: the enemy's army was too strong.
games.why: the Talmud says baseless hatred: people hating each other for nothing. so the day of mourning becomes a call to repair.

practice: If it's comfortable, lower yourself to the floor; if not, sit low in a chair. Think of one loss you carry, big or small; you don't have to fix it, just let the ground hold you while you hold it.
If you pray, you can say Lamentations' old line: renew our days.
